statement: In people who use ecstasy and are abstinent when tested, compared with people who do not use it, memory and executive test scores are on average lower. The figures available in the sources read here are second-hand, as summarized by two narrative reviews and a letter: in one meta-analysis of 26 studies, standardized differences of d -0.63 (short-term memory), -0.87 (long-term memory), -1.00 (verbal memory) and -0.27 (visual memory); in a larger review, pooled differences on six memory measures against both people who do not use drugs and people who use other drugs, with no difference in crystallized intelligence. Individual studies are mixed, most simple tasks are not affected, and most working-memory tasks are normal apart from updating and some visuospatial tasks. None of the primary studies or meta-analyses was read, no intervals or heterogeneity statistics are reported, and whether ecstasy caused the differences is a separate, contested question. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: People who use ecstasy score lower on average on memory and thinking tests than people who do not. The sizes come from reviews, not from the studies themselves, and the studies disagree with one another. Simple tasks are mostly normal. These studies cannot show that ecstasy caused the difference.
population: Adults who use ecstasy recreationally and were abstinent when tested (duration of abstinence mostly not stated in the sources read)
comparator: People who have not used ecstasy, or who use other drugs but not ecstasy
outcome: Memory and executive neuropsychological test scores
magnitude: Second-hand, as summarized in the sources read: memory domain differences of about 0.3 to 1.0 SD (d -0.63 short-term, -0.87 long-term, -1.00 verbal, -0.27 visual memory; 26 studies, Laws and Kokkalis, 2007, as summarized); pooled differences on six memory measures against both comparison groups and none on IQ (Rogers et al., 2009, as summarized), with pooled p=0.017 for digit span and p<0.001 for a verbal immediate-recall composite over 27 studies. No confidence intervals, heterogeneity statistics or publication-bias assessments are given in the sources read.

evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: a meta-analysis of 26 studies with calculable effect sizes (Laws and Kokkalis, 2007) gave Cohen's d of -0.63 for short-term memory, -0.87 for long-term memory, -1.00 for verbal memory and -0.27 for visual memory; a review of over one hundred neurocognitive studies (Rogers et al., 2009) found differences against both people who do not use drugs and people who use other drugs, varying in strength by task; a third review (Nulsen et al., 2010) reported poorer performance in all memory domains.

evidence.locator: §3.5 Neurocognition: the contributory role of other psychoactive drugs, 3rd paragraph (proof lines 587-605)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: in the same review (Rogers et al., 2009), seven variables had enough studies for meta-analysis; on all six memory measures (RAVLT immediate and delayed word recall, Rivermead immediate and delayed prose recall, digit span forwards and backwards) the ecstasy group scored lower than both people who do not use drugs and people who use other drugs, while the seventh, IQ, did not differ from the polydrug comparison group; differences were generally largest against people who do not use drugs.

evidence.locator: 2nd paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the letter from the same meta-analysis: marked variation across studies; pooled digit span lower than in people who use other drugs (P=0.017); a pooled verbal immediate-recall composite lower over 27 published studies (P<0.001); 6 of the 7 meta-analysed variables lower, with NART IQ the exception.

As summarized: a review of 33 published studies of working memory (Murphy et al., 2009) found performance normal in most studies, executive-shifting and most inhibition tasks unaffected, and differences mainly on tasks requiring the updating of verbal information and on visuospatial tasks needing processing beyond storage and retrieval.

The review states that many simple cognitive skills are not affected and that even on tasks that often show differences these are not universally found: in the meta-analysis it cites, individual studies of digit span and of a verbal immediate-recall composite were a mixture of significant and non-significant results although the pooled estimates were significant; the author attributes the variation to lifetime dose, sample size, participant selection and control of error variance.

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional comparisons, seen only through narrative reviews and a letter that do not appraise them; groups differ in other drug use and probably in education and premorbid ability, which the sources read do not report.

inconsistency.note: The sources themselves describe a mixture of significant and non-significant individual studies on the same tasks.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the figures come from reviews of reviews; no primary study and no meta-analysis was read here (METHODS §6.3).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: no funnel or small-study analysis is reported in the sources read.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low. Downgraded for risk of bias (unappraised cross-sectional comparisons with confounding by other drug use and unmeasured premorbid ability), inconsistency (the reviews report mixed individual studies) and indirectness (figures are second-hand from narrative reviews). The claim is rated as an association; whether ecstasy caused the difference is the contested question in section 14.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on narrative reviews and a letter; stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). The editor should replace these anchors with the meta-analyses and primary studies when they are read.

changelog.change: Drafted from the MDMA batch 1 reviews and letters (reader25): second-hand effect sizes for memory and executive tests.

statement: When people who use ecstasy are selected for minimal use of other drugs and compared with people from the same all-night-dance scene who have not used ecstasy, most test scores do not differ. As described second-hand in the sources read here, one such study of 52 people who used ecstasy and 59 who did not gave 15 tests: five differed between the whole groups at p of 0.05 or below (spatial span forwards, digit-symbol, vocabulary, digits backwards and the grooved pegboard with the non-dominant hand), without correction for multiple comparisons, and in the heavier-use subgroup a strategy-application test and the non-dominant-hand pegboard differed at p=0.003. The same results are read in opposite ways by the two commentaries read here: as evidence of lasting harm, and as evidence against it with the one consistent difference attributed to traits that precede drug use. The primary study was not read for this claim. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: In one study, people who used ecstasy but hardly any other drugs scored much like people who had never used it. A few of the 15 tests were lower, and two experts read the same results in opposite ways. We have read only their descriptions, not the study itself.
population: Adults who use ecstasy with minimal lifetime use of other illicit drugs and alcohol, abstinent when tested (median 121 days since last use in the study described)
exposure: Recreational ecstasy use (median 43.5 lifetime occasions in the study described)
comparator: People who have not used ecstasy, recruited from the same all-night-dance scene
magnitude: As described second-hand: of 15 tests, five differed between the whole groups with p values of 0.04, 0.02, 0.01, 0.05 and 0.02 (uncorrected); in the subgroup with 50 or more lifetime occasions, a strategy-application test and the non-dominant-hand pegboard differed at p=0.003; the lighter and heavier subgroups did not generally differ, and on some measures the lighter subgroup scored lower. No effect sizes are given in the sources read.

evidence.extracted: As listed by the letter from the study's Table 2: Wechsler Memory Scale spatial span forwards P<0.04, WAIS digit-symbol P<0.02, WAIS vocabulary P<0.01, WAIS digits backwards P<0.05 and grooved pegboard with the non-dominant hand P<0.02. The letter rejects the study authors' reading that such differences are probably chance findings from uncorrected multiple comparisons, and notes that trail-making B and California verbal learning, which it says are often impaired, did not differ.

As described: with moderate use defined as fewer than 50 and heavy use as 50 or more lifetime occasions, the two subgroups did not generally differ and on some measures the moderate subgroup scored lower; only 6 of the 22 people in the heavier subgroup had used on 150 or more occasions, and the subgroups' lifetime use was not reported. The grooved pegboard did not differ with the dominant hand; with the non-dominant hand the whole ecstasy group was slower (P=0.02) and the heavier subgroup more so (P=0.003 against controls), which the study's authors judged probably chance.

As described by the commentary: of 15 neuropsychological tests, chosen because other studies had reported differences on them, only the Revised Strategy Applications Test clearly showed poorer performance, in the heavier-use subgroup but not the moderate one; the ecstasy group was selected for low exposure to other illicit drugs and alcohol, controls came from the same all-night-dance scene, and the analyses adjusted for demographic factors and childhood attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

The commentary argues that poorer strategic self-regulation fits traits that precede drug use: lower serotonergic function has been linked to impulsivity, impulsivity to lower prefrontal activation, reward sensitivity and heavier substance use, and one prospective study found that decision-making performance in people who had not used ecstasy predicted later first use.

The review describes three studies of people with minimal other drug use: in a 2004 pilot study the lighter subgroup did not differ from controls while the heavier subgroup scored lower on Wisconsin card sorting, Stroop interference and a strategy test; in a Hong Kong study that excluded people with illicit polydrug histories, basic working memory was normal and verbal memory, non-verbal memory and complex attention were poorer; for the 2011 study the review says the whole group had few differences and attributes spatial span forwards and digit span backwards to the heavier subgroup, which the study's own tables do not show (see the card's reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.note: One cross-sectional study, known to this claim only through commentaries that disagree about its results and one of which misreports them; no pre-use measurement, and the group difference in vocabulary suggests differences that predate use.

inconsistency.note: Only one study; the disagreement is about interpretation, not about the numbers.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the primary study was not read for this claim, and the sample (people with unusually light use of other drugs) is not typical of people who use ecstasy.

imprecision.note: 52 against 59 people, 22 in the heavier subgroup; 15 tests without correction; no effect sizes in the sources read.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low, downgraded for risk of bias (no pre-use baseline, uncorrected multiple comparisons, descriptions that conflict with the study's tables), indirectness (second-hand, and an atypically light-use sample) and imprecision (one small study). The editor should re-anchor this claim on the primary study, which the other reader of this batch has. The two published readings of this study (a letter reading it as evidence of harm, a commentary reading it as evidence against, with the one consistent difference attributed to traits that precede use) are summarized in the anchors and in the section 14 debate box.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on a letter, a commentary and a narrative review; stays at draft (METHODS §6.3) until anchored on the primary study.

changelog.change: Drafted from the two 2011 commentaries and the 2013 review (reader25); the primary study is with the other reader of this batch. Kept as a single-study claim rather than a second debate box: the disagreement over this study is carried in the contested claim of section 14, and the two readings are stated here.

statement: In people who had not used ecstasy when first tested, those who then began using it scored lower than people who did not at the second testing, on verbal memory in one cohort and on figural visual recognition in another. The figures here are second-hand, as summarized by a narrative review: 58 people who used an average of 3.2 ecstasy tablets against 60 who used none, with no difference at baseline and poorer immediate and delayed verbal recall and verbal recognition at follow-up; and 23 people who used an average of 13.5 tablets over a year against 43 people who used cannabis, with most tasks not differing. The review misstates the retest interval of the first cohort and omits that its authors reported the scores as remaining within the normal range; the primary studies were not read for this claim. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Two studies tested people before they had ever used ecstasy and again later. Those who started using scored a little lower on some memory tests than those who did not. The numbers here come from a review that got one detail wrong, so they need checking against the studies.
population: Young adults who had not used ecstasy when first tested and began using it before the second testing
exposure: Starting ecstasy use (a mean of 3.2 tablets in total in one cohort; a mean of 13.5 tablets over a year in the other)
comparator: People in the same cohorts who did not start using ecstasy (one comparison group used cannabis)
outcome: Change in neuropsychological test scores between the two testings
magnitude: Second-hand and without effect sizes: in the first cohort (58 against 60 people), no baseline difference and lower immediate and delayed verbal recall and verbal recognition at follow-up; in the second (23 against 43), most tasks did not differ and figural visual recognition, immediate and delayed, was poorer. No intervals are given in the source read.

evidence.extracted: As summarized: of 149 people almost naive to ecstasy at baseline, 23 who had used a mean of 13.5 tablets over the following year were compared with 43 people who used cannabis; most tasks did not differ, but figural visual recognition (immediate and delayed) was poorer (Wagner et al., 2013). Of 188 people who had not used ecstasy, 58 who then used an average of 3.2 tablets were compared with 60 who did not; there was no neurocognitive difference at baseline, and at follow-up the ecstasy group had poorer immediate and delayed verbal recall and verbal recognition (Schilt et al., 2007). The review gives the retest interval as 18-36 months, which is wrong by the editors' check against the primary paper (Schilt et al., 2007, PDF p. 731: mean 11.1 months in the ecstasy group and 19.1 months in the control group).

As summarized: 15 people tested a year apart, whose average lifetime use rose from 19 to 55 occasions, declined on Rivermead paragraph recall but not on two Wechsler subtests; at 2 years, the 8 who had stopped were unchanged or better (overall Rivermead memory score 19.9 to 22.9) and the 7 who continued were unchanged or worse (17.4 to 9.2). There was no retested comparison group, so practice effects cannot be separated from change.

As summarized from the same prospective programme: 188 people who had not used ecstasy were followed, and the 59 who had used it by the 17-month follow-up (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2.0) were compared with 56 who had not; serotonin transporter binding did not differ, which the review attributes to the very low use, while measures of cerebral blood volume, fractional anisotropy and apparent diffusion differed (de Win et al., 2008).

risk_of_bias.note: Prospective, but people chose whether to start using; the cohorts differed in other drug use and, in the first, in the interval between testings; the source read reports no adjustment detail and misstates that interval.

inconsistency.note: Two cohorts, different tests affected; too few studies to judge heterogeneity.

indirectness.note: Second-hand from a narrative review; very low doses, so the findings do not speak to heavier patterns of use.

imprecision.note: 58 against 60 and 23 against 43 people, with no effect sizes or intervals in the source read.

grade.reasoning: Prospective observational evidence starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias (self-selection into use, unequal retest intervals, no adjustment detail in the source), indirectness (second-hand and very low doses) and imprecision (small cohorts, no intervals). The review's description contains an error on the retest interval, so the claim must be re-anchored on the primary study, which the other reader of this batch has read.

verification.flag_note: Second-hand anchors only; stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). Replace with the primary cohort study's own anchors.

changelog.change: Drafted from the 2013 review's summary of two prospective cohorts (reader25), with the review's error on the retest interval recorded.

statement: In people who use ecstasy and are abstinent when scanned, binding of radioligands to the serotonin transporter is lower than in people who do not use it, in most but not all imaging studies. The figures here are second-hand, as summarized by a narrative review and a letter: in one study of 49 people who used ecstasy and 50 who did not, binding was lower throughout the cerebral cortex (-19% to -46%) and in the hippocampus (-21%), related to the extent of use and unchanged after control for the confounders the authors could address; in another, a group who preferred MDMA had lower binding in the neocortex (-56%), pallidostriatum (-19%) and amygdala (-32%), correlated with lifetime use, while a group who preferred hallucinogens showed none. In a prospective cohort with very low use, binding did not differ. What a lower binding signal means for nerve cells is disputed, and no primary imaging study was read for this claim. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Brain scans of people who use ecstasy often show less of a marker of serotonin nerve endings than scans of people who do not. The numbers here come from reviews, not from the scans themselves, and a lower signal does not by itself prove nerve cells were damaged.
population: Adults who use ecstasy recreationally, abstinent when scanned
exposure: Recreational ecstasy (MDMA) use, mostly moderate to heavy lifetime use
comparator: People who have not used ecstasy, or who use other drugs but not ecstasy
outcome: Serotonin transporter (SERT) binding measured with PET or SPECT
magnitude: Second-hand: -19% to -46% across cortical regions and -21% in the hippocampus (49 against 50 people, as summarized); -56% neocortex, -19% pallidostriatum, -32% amygdala in a group preferring MDMA, with no change in a group preferring hallucinogens. No intervals are given in the sources read, and one prospective cohort of people with very low use (59 against 56) found no difference.

evidence.locator: §2.2 'Serotonergic neurotoxicity' in humans: neuroimaging findings, 2nd paragraph (proof lines 186-210)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: 49 people with moderate ecstasy use against 50 people who did not use it; serotonin transporter binding lower in every cortical region (range -19% to -46%) and in the hippocampus (-21%), related to years of use and maximum dose; recent use checked by hair analysis, with other drug use, sex, a gene polymorphism and chronic tolerance monitored; the occipital lobe showed the largest mean reduction (46%) in a caudorostral gradient (Kish et al., 2010).

As summarized: a group who preferred MDMA showed lower serotonin transporter binding potential in the neocortex (-56%), pallidostriatum (-19%) and amygdala (-32%), with the extent correlated with lifetime MDMA exposure, while a group who preferred hallucinogens (mainly LSD) showed no change (Erritzoe et al., 2011); a post-mortem case of one person who had used ecstasy as well as cocaine and heroin had striatal serotonin 60% to 77% below normal with normal dopamine (Kish et al., 2000).

The review states that not every imaging study found reductions, that the variation has been attributed to lifetime dose, duration of abstinence, radioligand, brain region, sex, polydrug use and sample size, and that the early evidence was criticized in the mid-2000s over the specificity of the markers for serotonin and other methodological issues, before reviews concluded that lower serotonin transporter density was the most robust finding.

As summarized: in a prospective cohort, the 59 people who had used ecstasy by the 17-month follow-up (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2.0) did not differ in serotonin transporter binding from 56 people who had not, which the review attributes to the very low lifetime dose; the study's authors concluded that they could not exclude that even low doses are neurotoxic, and reported differences in cerebral blood volume, fractional anisotropy and apparent diffusion.

evidence.locator: 8th paragraph (p. 1366 right column, continued on p. 1367)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the letter: a review of the neuroimaging literature (the letter's reference 23) concluded that reduced serotonin transporter density was the most robust finding; a study of 49 people abstinent from ecstasy and 50 people who did not use it found binding lower in every cortical region (-19% to -46%) and the hippocampus (-21%), associated with cumulative lifetime use and maximum use on one occasion, persisting after control for confounds including other drug use, and correlated with cognitive performance.

The author of a cross-sectional imaging study writes that MDMA has a well-established ability to cause serotonin neurotoxicity in non-human primates and that he is not aware of evidence that humans are less vulnerable, while accepting that traits such as impulsivity may predispose people to use MDMA; he gives no human measurement in support.

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional imaging comparisons with no pre-use scan, small samples and self-reported exposure, seen only through sources that do not appraise them.

inconsistency.note: The reviews themselves report that not every study found reductions, and a prospective cohort with very low use found none.

indirectness.note: Second-hand figures, and a binding signal is a surrogate: it can change without loss of nerve terminals.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the percentages are group differences in a surrogate marker between small selected samples (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Not applied: the dose relationships are reported second-hand and come from the same cross-sectional samples.

grade.reasoning: Observational imaging evidence starts low, downgraded for risk of bias (no pre-use scan, small selected samples), inconsistency (studies disagree, including a prospective cohort with no difference) and indirectness (second-hand, and the marker is a surrogate for terminal integrity). The claim is worded as an association in a measurement, not as damage.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on a narrative review, a letter and a correspondence; stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). The imaging studies themselves (Kish et al., 2010; Erritzoe et al., 2011; McCann et al., 2008; de Win et al., 2008) are not in this batch and should be read before this claim is shown.

changelog.change: Drafted (reader25) because the batch's question turns on the serotonin system but no primary imaging study was assigned; all figures are second-hand and marked as such.

statement: A 2002 report in Science that a common recreational dose regimen of MDMA caused severe dopaminergic neurotoxicity in primates was retracted in September 2003, its authors reporting that a labelling error meant all but one animal had received methamphetamine instead; this is as described by the two sources read here, not from the paper or the retraction notice. A case study of the 50 largest US newspapers with searchable archives found that 26 (52%) covered the publication and 20 (40%) the retraction; of the 26 that covered the publication, 14 (54%) covered the retraction, and 6 newspapers covered only the retraction. Retraction stories were shorter on average (mean 396 against 482 words), and all 20 stated both that the original findings had suggested that one night's use could cause brain damage or parkinsonism and that a mix-up of compounds made them erroneous. The difference in coverage between the two events was not tested by the authors. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In 2002 a study said that one night's worth of ecstasy damaged monkeys' brains. A year later it was withdrawn: the monkeys had been given the wrong drug by mistake. Of 50 big US newspapers, 26 wrote about the study and 20 about the withdrawal.
population: The 50 largest US newspapers with searchable online archives (frame taken from a 2007 circulation ranking, descended to rank 64 where archives were missing)
exposure: Publication of the 2002 primate report, and its retraction in September 2003
comparator: Coverage of the retraction compared with coverage of the publication in the same newspapers
outcome: Whether a newspaper published a story, the length of the stories, and the elements the retraction stories contained
magnitude: Publication covered by 26 of 50 newspapers (52%; editors' calculation, Wilson 95% CI 38.5% to 65.2%) and the retraction by 20 of 50 (40%; 27.6% to 53.8%); 14 of the 26 that covered the publication also covered the retraction (54%; 35.5% to 71.2%), and 6 of 50 (12%) covered only the retraction. Mean lengths 482 words (SD 303) for publication stories and 396 (SD 193) for retraction stories. Neither difference was tested by the authors; editors' calculations give exact McNemar p=0.24 for the coverage difference (12 against 6 discordant newspapers) and Welch p=0.25 for the word counts.

evidence.extracted: As the authors describe the 2002 study: published in Science in September 2002 by Ricaurte, McCann and colleagues at Johns Hopkins University, funded by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse; MDMA was given to 10 non-human primates to model human use; imaging was reported to show severe dopaminergic and less severe serotonergic neurotoxicity, and the authors of the case study state that two of the animals died. The dopaminergic finding was new and raised the possibility of parkinsonism.

As described: in September 2003, one year after publication, Science issued a retraction in which Ricaurte and colleagues wrote that they had discovered that methamphetamine rather than MDMA had been used to treat all but one study animal, because of a labelling error; the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies then asked the funding institute to investigate all work done by the group since the mislabelled supply had been received.

Of 50 newspapers, 26 (52%) published a report on the publication and 20 (40%) on the retraction; 6 (12%) covered the retraction without having covered the publication; of the 26 that covered the publication, 14 (54%) covered the retraction. Circulation size was not associated with coverage of the publication (p=.25) or of the retraction (p=.84).

Mean word count 482 (SD 303; range 69 to 1260) for publication stories and 396 (SD 193; range 86 to 837) for retraction stories; in the 14 newspapers covering both events, 550 (SD 271) against 386 (SD 205). No test of these differences is reported.

All 20 retraction stories reported that the original findings had suggested that one night's MDMA use could cause brain damage or parkinsonism, and that a mix-up of study compounds had made the results erroneous. Fewer gave context: 14 (70%) mentioned long-standing controversy, 13 (65%) earlier criticism, 11 (55%) that animals died, 7 (35%) earlier research suggesting serotonergic damage, 7 (35%) allegations of political motives and 4 (20%) a quotation from a critic. No component differed significantly between the 14 newspapers covering both events and the 6 covering only the retraction (Fisher's exact test, p from 0.06 to 1.00).

evidence.locator: Letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin (left column); Response, 1st paragraph (middle column)
evidence.extracted: Three months before the retraction, critics argued that the high mortality among the primates showed the regimen was not a common recreational one and called the interspecies scaling into question; the study's authors replied that interspecies scaling had not been used in these studies and that one of ten monkeys given the regimen had died of complications related to hyperthermia, from which they judged it premature to draw conclusions about mortality.

The authors note that the publication was accompanied by a university announcement and a press release from the publisher's association, that the retraction was issued late on a Friday afternoon, giving low-key coverage (quoting a journal editorial), and list as limitations that archives could not be searched for all of the 50 largest US newspapers, that the press release for the retraction could not be obtained, and that the placement of stories within newspapers was not analysed.

risk_of_bias.note: Archive searches were not validated and 14 of the 64 largest newspapers were skipped for lack of archives; the content coding has no stated scheme, coder or reliability; both authors have a declared stake in how MDMA research is portrayed, and a missed retraction story would move the figures in the direction they report.

inconsistency.note: One case study; nothing to compare it with here.

indirectness.note: The counts describe exactly the newspapers named. What the 2002 paper claimed and why it was retracted is second-hand and is stated in the claim as these sources describe it, not rated here.

imprecision.note: Intervals are wide (about 14 percentage points either way) but the claim reports them.

large_effect.note: Descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim about one set of newspapers, rated as a description of the population sampled (METHODS §6.3). It starts low and is downgraded once for risk of bias: unvalidated archive searching, missing archives, unreported coding and authors with a stake in the subject. The retraction itself is a documented event, but neither the 2002 paper nor its retraction notice was read, so the claim says it is as these sources describe it.

verification.flag_note: The retraction notice (Science 2003;301:1479) and the 2002 paper should be added as references and read before this claim is shown to readers.

changelog.change: Drafted (reader25) from the newspaper case study and the 2003 Science correspondence; the editors' intervals and tests are labelled as calculations.

statement: Whether MDMA damages dopamine neurons in people has not been shown. The one report that claimed it, a 2002 primate study, was retracted after its authors found that all but one animal had received methamphetamine; as described in the 2021 case study read here, evidence of MDMA-induced dopaminergic toxicity in humans has not appeared since, although that statement is made without citing human studies. In the 2003 exchange that preceded the retraction, the critics cited imaging and post-mortem reports of normal dopamine markers in people who used MDMA heavily, and the study's authors replied that cerebrospinal fluid homovanillic acid is neither a sensitive nor a specific marker of dopamine neurotoxicity and that groups unselected for pattern of use would not be expected to show differences. No primary human study of dopamine markers was read for this claim. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does ecstasy harm the brain's dopamine cells in people? There is no good evidence that it does. The one study that said so was withdrawn because the animals had been given a different drug by mistake.
comparator: People who have not used ecstasy
outcome: Damage to dopamine neurons or lasting change in dopamine markers
magnitude: Not estimable from the sources read: they contain no human dopamine measurements, only each side's description of studies not read here.

evidence.locator: Letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin (left column), middle of the paragraph
evidence.extracted: The critics state that studies finding normal dopamine, with reduced serotonin, in people who used MDMA heavily were not cited by the primate paper: two studies using in vivo imaging of the dopamine transporter and one post-mortem examination of one person; and that earlier studies by the same research group in people who used MDMA heavily did not find reduced dopamine metabolites in cerebrospinal fluid.

The study's authors reply that because the human studies cited did not take patterns of use into account, the groups were probably heterogeneous and dopamine markers, including the transporter, would not be expected to differ; and that cerebrospinal fluid homovanillic acid is neither a sensitive nor a specific marker of dopamine neurotoxicity, so it would not be expected to be reduced even in a homogeneous group.

The authors state that evidence of MDMA-induced dopaminergic toxicity in humans has not materialized since the retraction, and that regulatory agencies have judged MDMA's potential therapeutic benefits to outweigh its risks in research settings; the only source given for these sentences is a 2014 commentary co-authored by one of them.

The dopaminergic finding in the 2002 primate study was new and raised the possibility of parkinsonism after recreational use; the paper was retracted in September 2003 because, as its authors then reported, a labelling error meant that all but one animal had received methamphetamine rather than MDMA.

risk_of_bias.note: The sources are letters and a media case study by authors on both sides of the dispute; the negative statement is an assertion without citation of human studies, and the critics' description of the cerebrospinal fluid literature does not hold for at least one of the studies they cite (see card sc_mithoefer_2003, reporting issues).

indirectness.note: No human dopamine measurement was read; everything here is each side's description of studies not read, and the retracted evidence was from primates.

imprecision.note: Not applicable: no estimate is made, and the claim says the question is unresolved rather than that there is no effect.

grade.reasoning: Starts low as observational evidence and is downgraded for risk of bias (partisan letters, an uncited assertion) and indirectness (no human dopamine data were read). The claim says only that the question has not been settled; absence of evidence here is not evidence of absence, because none of the human studies on either side was read.

debate.question: Does recreational MDMA use damage dopamine nerve cells in people?
debate.evidence_yes: The case for a dopamine effect rested on the 2002 primate report of severe dopaminergic neurotoxicity after what its title called a common recreational dose regimen, and on its authors' argument that the pattern of dosing, not only the amount, decides which transmitter systems are affected, so that three doses given over several hours produced damage to both dopamine and serotonin systems while more widely spaced, higher doses produced serotonin damage alone (Ricaurte and colleagues, reply to Mithoefer et al., 2003). They also pointed to mouse evidence of MDMA-related dopamine neurotoxicity, and argued that human studies which ignore patterns of use would not be expected to show differences in dopamine markers. That report was retracted in September 2003 (as described by Barnett and Doblin, 2021), so this side of the argument no longer has its primary support.
debate.evidence_no: The critics cited human studies finding normal dopamine with reduced serotonin in people who used MDMA heavily: two in vivo imaging studies of the dopamine transporter, one post-mortem examination, and earlier work by the same research group reporting dopamine metabolites in cerebrospinal fluid that were not reduced (Mithoefer et al., 2003). They also argued that the high mortality among the primates showed the regimen was not a common recreational one. The newspaper case study states that evidence of MDMA-induced dopaminergic toxicity in humans has not appeared in the years since the retraction (Barnett and Doblin, 2021).
debate.neither_can_show: None of the human studies on either side was read for this claim, and neither the 2002 paper nor its retraction notice is among the sources. Both documents are partisan: one letter is from people who ran and defended the study, the other from an organization that funds MDMA therapy research and asked for an investigation. The critics' description of the cerebrospinal fluid literature is not accurate for at least one study they cite, in which the dopamine metabolite homovanillic acid was lower in the MDMA group overall and in women (see card sc_mithoefer_2003). A statement that evidence has not materialized is an argument from silence: no systematic search is reported behind it.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The claim that recreational MDMA damages dopamine neurons in people rested on a study that was withdrawn because the animals had mostly received a different drug, and no human evidence for it has been put before us. That is not the same as showing that MDMA leaves dopamine systems untouched: the human studies cited on both sides have not been read here, their samples were small and unselected for pattern of use, and the markers used (transporter binding, a metabolite in spinal fluid) can change without loss of nerve cells. The honest position is that the question is open and that the burden rests with anyone asserting either answer.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Dopamine transporter or vesicular transporter imaging, and post-mortem dopamine markers, in people with documented heavy MDMA use and little stimulant use, against matched controls, with the pattern of use recorded and repeat measurement over abstinence; and a systematic search of the human literature published since 2003, which none of the sources read here reports.

verification.flag_note: Rests on letters and a media case study; stays at draft. Needs the human dopamine-marker studies and the retraction notice before it can rise.

changelog.change: Drafted (reader25) to carry the dopamine side of the retraction question, which the memory and serotonin claims do not cover.

statement: Whether recreational ecstasy use causes lasting damage to the serotonin system in people, and whether any such damage explains the lower test scores found in people who use it, is contested and not settled by the sources read in this batch, which are narrative reviews, letters and commentaries rather than primary studies. On one side, reviews report lower serotonin transporter binding in most imaging studies and lower memory and executive scores in many studies, often related to lifetime use. On the other, commentators point out that no study in this literature measured people before they began using, that traits such as impulsivity predict who starts, that a study of people with minimal use of other drugs found few differences, and that the descriptions of individual studies in these reviews are at points inaccurate. The authors on both sides agree that prospective studies are needed; the figures here are second-hand. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does ecstasy damage the brain's serotonin system for good? Experts disagree, and the papers read here are opinion pieces and reviews, not new studies. Nobody has tested people before they started using, so a difference found later could have been there all along.
comparator: People who have not used ecstasy
outcome: Lasting damage to serotonin neurons, and cognitive consequences attributed to it
magnitude: Not estimable from these sources. The quantities they report are second-hand: serotonin transporter binding lower by 19% to 46% across cortical regions in one study (49 against 50 people), memory differences of about 0.3 to 1.0 SD in one meta-analysis of 26 studies, and few differences on 15 tests in one study of people with minimal use of other drugs (52 against 59).

evidence.extracted: The review states that serotonergic neurotoxicity after MDMA is well established in laboratory animals, that imaging studies have found lower serotonin transporter binding in abstinent people who use ecstasy, that declarative memory, prospective memory and higher cognitive skills are often impaired, that the differences are often related to lifetime dose, with slight changes in light use and more pronounced problems in heavy use, and that abstinent people who use ecstasy can show deficits across a wide range of functions with a serotonergic component.

evidence.locator: §6.2 MDMA and serotonergic neurotoxicity: current explanatory model, 6th paragraph (proof lines 1522-1539)
evidence.extracted: The same review states that whether the problems endure over time cannot be answered on current evidence, that there are some indications that they endure but the empirical data are very limited, and that prospective studies combining neuroimaging with a comprehensive battery of functional measures are needed to address this question.

evidence.locator: §2.1 Serotonergic neurotoxicity in laboratory animals, 2nd paragraph (proof lines 141-158)
evidence.extracted: The review reports that the predominant hypothesis for the animal findings is loss of the end regions of long serotonin axons, that other interpretations including neuroadaptive change without terminal loss should be considered, and that the authors it cites called for a clearer definition of neurotoxicity while concluding that MDMA can be called neurotoxic in the sense of causing serotonergic dysfunction.

The letter concludes that the modest cognitive differences found in a study of people with minimal use of other drugs are congruent with current understanding of MDMA, that in the author's bio-energetic stress model MDMA is most damaging when taken intensively and cumulatively, and that the study confirms MDMA's potential for causing neurobiological damage even when taken carefully.

The commentary states that the evidence for functional signs of serotonergic neurotoxicity in people who use ecstasy remains mixed, that transporter deficiencies in people who use ecstasy appear to recover with abstinence whereas they persist years after fenfluramine use, that the two possibilities cannot be disentangled in retrospective studies, and that within-person comparison before and after controlled exposure is the way to resolve it, the few such examples so far showing no resulting deficits.
evidence.quote: the chimera of MDMA-induced neurotoxicity in human ecstasy users may finally be put to rest

evidence.extracted: The author of a cross-sectional imaging study agrees with his critics on the need for well-controlled longitudinal studies to address the potential neurotoxic effects of recreational MDMA, and concludes that large, well-controlled prospective studies are needed to confirm or refute the findings of cross-sectional studies, while holding that well-designed cross-sectional studies remain informative.

The same author reports that his critics re-analysed his raw data by combining the MDMA group and the control group in one correlation and found no association between MDMA exposure and brain activation; he replies that people with little use tend to fall below the control mean and people with much use above it, so that including controls obscures the dose relationship. Neither analysis is given in numbers.

The authors state that debate continues about the safety of MDMA, including whether serotonergic damage associated with recreational use applies to pharmaceutical-grade MDMA and whether long-term neurocognitive deficits exist, citing among others the two 2011 commentaries and the reviews read in this batch.

risk_of_bias.note: All sources are reviews, letters or commentaries by authors with declared positions; none appraises the studies it cites, and the review's descriptions of individual studies contain errors (see card sc_parrott_2013).

inconsistency.note: Counted once, under risk of bias: the disagreement is about the interpretation of a largely shared body of cross-sectional studies, not about separate findings.

indirectness.note: Second-hand throughout; the outcome of interest (lasting damage to nerve cells) is inferred from binding signals and test scores.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources, though their selection of studies is unsystematic on both sides.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence seen only through narrative reviews and commentaries starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias (no appraisal, partisan selection, errors in description) and indirectness (second-hand, surrogate outcomes). The claim is worded as insufficient evidence, which is what these sources support: their own authors call for prospective studies.

debate.question: Does recreational ecstasy use cause lasting damage to the brain's serotonin system in people, and does that damage explain the lower test scores found in people who use it?
debate.evidence_yes: A narrative review sets out the case: serotonergic neurotoxicity after MDMA is well established in laboratory animals; most human imaging studies report lower serotonin transporter binding in people abstinent from ecstasy, by 19% to 46% across cortical regions and 21% in the hippocampus in one study of 49 people against 50 (as summarized), related to lifetime use and surviving control for other drug use; a group preferring MDMA showed reductions while a group preferring hallucinogens showed none; memory and higher cognitive differences appear in many studies, with meta-analytic differences of about 0.3 to 1.0 SD, and are reported in relation to lifetime dose; and lower binding goes with poorer memory in two imaging studies (Parrott, 2013). A letter adds that differences appear even in people who use almost no other drugs, and reads this as showing damage under conditions the author calls protective (Parrott, 2011). The author of a cross-sectional imaging study holds that MDMA's serotonin neurotoxicity in non-human primates is well established, that he knows of no evidence that humans are less vulnerable, and that incident use was followed by increased impulsivity in a prospective cohort (Cowan, 2012).
debate.evidence_no: No study in this literature measured people before they began using, so differences that predate use cannot be excluded; traits such as impulsivity and weaker executive control are linked to lower serotonergic function and to heavier substance use, and decision-making predicted first ecstasy use in a prospective study, so the heaviest-using groups would score lower even with no drug effect (Lyvers, 2011). In the study designed to remove confounding by other drugs, only one of 15 tests clearly differed, and only in the heavier-use subgroup (Lyvers, 2011). Transporter binding in people who use ecstasy appears to recover with abstinence, unlike the persistent reductions reported years after fenfluramine, a drug prescribed to millions (Lyvers, 2011). Re-analysis of one imaging study's raw data, combining the MDMA group with controls, found no association between exposure and brain activation (as reported by Cowan, 2012). Not every imaging study finds reductions, and a prospective cohort of people with very low use found no transporter difference (Parrott, 2013). The animal literature itself admits an interpretation without loss of nerve terminals, and the field has been criticized for lacking a clear definition of neurotoxicity (Parrott, 2013).
debate.neither_can_show: Nothing read here is a primary study: these are reviews, letters and commentaries, and their descriptions of individual studies differ from one another and, at points, from the studies' own tables. No design in this literature can separate a difference that follows use from one that preceded it, because no one has scanned or tested people before they started. Binding signals and test scores are surrogates: both can change without any loss of nerve cells, and neither side reports post-mortem or structural evidence in people. Group averages are reported without saying how many individuals fall outside the normal range, and the reviews report no formal assessment of publication bias. The two sides also select differently: the review omits the published critiques, and the commentary omits the transporter imaging studies.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From these sources alone, two things are well attested: a measurable difference in serotonin transporter binding between people who use ecstasy and people who do not, found by several groups, and a modest average difference in memory and executive test scores. Neither establishes lasting damage to nerve cells, and neither is shown to be caused by ecstasy: the designs cannot do it, the exposure is self-reported, and other drug use and pre-existing differences run in the same direction. The strongest argument on the yes side is the relation of both measures to lifetime use; the strongest on the no side is that the one study designed to remove confounding by other drugs found almost nothing, and that the traits in question predict who starts using. The authors on both sides agree that prospective studies are needed, which is the clearest signal of where this stands.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that measure serotonin transporter binding and cognition in people before first use and repeatedly afterwards, with use verified biologically, a retested group who do not start, and pre-specified outcomes; repeat scanning of the same people over years of abstinence to see whether binding and scores change together; within-person studies of controlled administration with the same measures; and post-mortem studies of structural markers in people with documented long-term use. None of the sources read here reports any of these.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on narrative reviews and commentaries; stays at draft (METHODS §6.3) and says so in its statement. The debate box is written from this batch's reviews and letters only; the primary studies and the systematic review of abstinence are with the other reader.

changelog.change: Drafted (reader25) as the contested question of section 14, from the reviews, letters and commentaries of MDMA batch 1 only.
